column2: The third prefatory discussion: on the temperate and the deviant zones, and the effect of the air on the colors of human beings and on many of their conditions

We have already shown that the settled part of this uncovered portion of the earth is only its middle, because of the excess of heat in the south of it and of cold in the north. Since the two sides, north and south, are opposites in heat and cold, the quality must pass by degrees from each of them toward the middle, so that the middle is temperate. The fourth zone is therefore the most temperate part of the settled world; the zones flanking it, the third and the fifth, are closer to temperateness; the zones next to these, the second and the sixth, are far from temperateness; and the first and the seventh are very much farther. For this reason the sciences, crafts, buildings, clothing, foods and fruits, and indeed the animals and everything else that comes into being in these three middle zones, are marked by temperateness, and their human inhabitants are more temperate in their bodies, colors, characters and religions, so that even prophecy is found, for the most part, only in them. We have not come across any report of a prophetic mission in the southern or the northern zones.

And that is because only the most perfect members of the species, in their physical make-up and their character, are singled out to be prophets and messengers. The Exalted said: “You are the best community brought forth for mankind” (3: 110). This is so that what the prophets bring them from God may be fully accepted. The people of these zones are more perfect because temperateness is found in them, and so you find them at the furthest point of moderation in their dwellings, clothing, foods and crafts. They make for themselves houses built up with stones embellished by craftsmanship; they vie with one another in seeking out the finest implements and vessels, and go to the limit in this. The natural metals are found among them: gold, silver, iron, copper, lead and tin. In their transactions they handle the two precious currencies, and in their conditions in general they keep away from deviation. These are the people of the Maghrib, Syria, the Hijaz, Yemen, the two Iraqs, India, Sind and China, and likewise al-Andalus and those near it among the Franks, the Galicians, the Rūm and the Greeks, and whoever is with these or close to them in these temperate zones. For this reason Iraq and Syria are the most temperate of all of these, because they lie in the middle from every direction.

As for the zones far from temperateness, such as the first, second, sixth and seventh, their people are farther from temperateness in all their conditions. Their buildings are of clay and reeds; their foods are sorghum and herbage; their clothing is of the leaves of trees, which they stitch together upon themselves, or of skins; and most of them go bare of any clothing. The fruits of their lands, and their relishes, are strange in their generation and inclined to deviation. Their transactions are carried on with something other than the two noble stones: with copper, iron or skins, to which they assign a value for use in transactions. Their characters, besides, are close to the nature of the speechless animals, so that it is reported of many of the black peoples (al-Sūdān) of the first zone that they live in caves and thickets, eat herbage, and are wild and untamed, eating one another; and the Slavs are likewise. The reason for this is that, because they are far from temperateness, the accidental qualities of their temperaments and characters come close to those of the speechless animals, and they are removed from humanity in proportion to that. Their religious conditions are likewise: they know no prophecy and follow no revealed law, except those of them who are near the edges of temperateness, and these are a rare and small minority, such as the Abyssinians, neighbors of Yemen, who followed Christianity before Islam and after it, down to the present time; such as the people of Mālī, Kūkū and Takrūr, neighbors of the land of the Maghrib, who follow Islam at the present time (it is said that they adopted it in the seventh century [AH]); and such as those who follow Christianity among the nations of the Slavs, the Franks and the Turks in the north.

And as for those other than these, among the people of those deviant zones in the south and the north, religion is unknown among them and knowledge is absent from them, and all their conditions are far from the conditions of human beings and close to the conditions of beasts. “And He creates what you do not know” (16: 8). This statement is not to be objected to on the ground that Yemen, Hadramawt, al-Aḥqāf, the lands of the Hijaz, al-Yamāma and what adjoins them of the Arabian Peninsula lie in the first and second zones. For the Arabian Peninsula is surrounded entirely by seas on three sides, as we mentioned, so that its moisture had an effect on the moisture of its air, which reduced the dryness and deviation that heat requires, and some temperateness came to be in it because of the moisture of the sea. Some genealogists, who have no knowledge of the natures of created things, have imagined that the black peoples are the descendants of Ham son of Noah, and that they were singled out for the color black because of a curse laid on him by his father, the effect of which appeared in his color and in the servitude that God placed in his progeny. They relate in this connection a tale taken from the fables of storytellers. Noah’s curse upon his son Ham does occur in the Torah, but it contains no mention of blackness; he called down upon him only that his children be slaves to the children of his brothers, and nothing more. To attribute blackness to Ham is to overlook the nature of heat and cold and their effect on the air and on the animals that come into being in it.

And that is because this color embraced the people of the first and second zones from the temper of their air, owing to the heat that is doubled in the south. The sun is at the zenith above their heads twice every year, the two times being close to each other, so that the period at the zenith lasts throughout the seasons; the light is therefore abundant because of it, the intense summer heat presses constantly upon them, and their skins turn black from the excess of heat. The counterparts of these two zones, in the north opposite them, are the seventh and the sixth; whiteness too embraced their inhabitants, from the temper of their air owing to the excessive cold in the north, since the sun always stays at their horizon, in the circle of the eye’s view or close to it, and never rises to the zenith or near it. Heat is therefore weak in them and the cold intense throughout the seasons, so that the colors of their people turn white and reach extreme pallor. There follow from this the things that the temper of excessive cold requires: blueness of the eyes, freckling of the skin and reddish-blond hair. Between these lie the three zones, the fifth, the fourth and the third, and these have an ample share of temperateness, which is the temper of the middle. The fourth of them reaches the furthest degree of temperateness, because it stands at the extreme point of the middle, as we explained before. Its people therefore had, in their physical make-up and character, as much temperateness as the temper of their airs required, and the third and the fifth followed it on its two sides, even though they did not reach the furthest point of moderation, since the one inclines slightly to the hot south and the other slightly to the cold north; yet they did not reach deviation. The four zones were deviant,

and their people are likewise deviant in their physical make-up and character: the first and the second for heat and blackness, and the seventh for cold and whiteness. The inhabitants of the south in the first and second zones are called by the names Abyssinians, Zanj and Sūdān, which are synonymous names for the nations changed by blackness, although the name Abyssinians is specific, among them, to those facing Mecca and Yemen, and Zanj to those facing the Indian Ocean. These names are not theirs because of descent from a black human being, whether Ham or anyone else. And we do find among the black peoples of the south some who settle in the temperate quarter or in the seventh zone, which inclines toward whiteness, and the colors of their descendants gradually turn white as the days pass; and the reverse holds for those of the people of the north, or of the fourth zone, who settle in the south, whose descendants’ colors turn black. In that is evidence that color follows the temper of the air. Ibn Sīnā said in his rajaz poem on medicine:
In the Zanj, heat changed the bodies ... until it clothed their skins in blackness / and the Slavs acquired whiteness ... until their skins became soft and fair

As for the people of the north, they were not named according to their colors, because whiteness was the color of the people of the language that laid down the names, so there was nothing strange in it that would lead to its being taken into account in naming, since it agreed with their own color and was familiar to them. We find its inhabitants, the Turks, the Slavs, the Ṭughurghur, the Khazars, the Alans, many of the Franks, and Gog and Magog, to be separate names and many different peoples, called by varied names. As for the people of the three middle zones, the people of temperateness in their physical make-up and way of life and in all the natural conditions of civilization among them — livelihood, dwellings, crafts, sciences, positions of leadership and royal authority — among them there were prophecy, royal authority, dynasties, revealed laws, sciences, towns, cities, buildings, discernment, excellent crafts and all the other temperate conditions. The people of these zones, whose reports we have come across, are such as the Arabs, the Rūm, the Persians, the Israelites, the Greeks, and the people of Sind, India and China. When the genealogists saw how these nations differed in their distinguishing marks and emblems, they supposed that this was because of lineages. So they made the people of the south all black peoples, descended from Ham, and since they were in doubt about their colors they went to the trouble of relating that flimsy tale; they made the people of the north, all or most of them, descendants of Japheth; and most of the temperate nations and the people of the middle, who profess the sciences, crafts, religions, revealed laws, statecraft and royal authority, descendants of Shem. This claim, even if it happens to coincide with the truth about the descent of these peoples, is not a rule that holds uniformly; it is only a report of what has actually occurred, and does not mean that the people of the south are called Sūdān and Abyssinians because of their descent from Ham the black.

And what led them to this error was only their belief that distinction between nations occurs only through lineages. It is not so: the distinction of a people or nation may be by lineage in some of them, as with the Arabs, the Israelites and the Persians; it may be by region and distinguishing mark, as with the Zanj, the Abyssinians, the Slavs and the Sūdān; and it may be by customs, emblems and lineage, as with the Arabs. And it may be by other conditions of nations, their particular qualities and distinguishing features. So to make a general statement about the people of a particular region, in the south or the north, that they are descended from such-and-such a known person, because of a creed or color or mark that embraces them and was found in that forefather, is one of the errors into which heedlessness of the natures of generated things and of regions has led them; for all these things change in later generations, and their continuing is not necessary. Such is God’s way with His servants, and “you will never find any change in God’s way.” God and His Messenger know best His unseen and are wiser, and He is the Protector, the Bestower of favors, the Kind, the Merciful.
